US midterm campaign enters final weekend as Alaska, California ballot fights heat up President Donald Trump's administration pressed a criminal investigation into Alaska’s pivotal US Senate race and said on Saturday it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, as the midterm campaign for control of Congress entered its final weekend. In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic ​challenger Mary Peltola helped to recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats’ hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday’s vote. Isolated clashes in France ​after peaceful marches, as police brace for Halloween night violence Scuffles broke out in Paris and other French cities on Saturday evening at the end of nationwide demonstrations driven by anger over living costs and ‌strained public services, while authorities ​warned of possible further violence overnight with Halloween celebrations under way. The protests, which were largely peaceful through the afternoon, continued for a third weekend after riots and looting on October 17 that caught security forces off guard, leaving a trail of damage to shops, public buildings and businesses across the country. US, Canada see growing interest in limited ceasefire in Black Sea US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Saturday said there was growing interest by the international community in facilitating a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea to ensure unfettered energy and grain shipments by Russia and Ukraine. Rubio told a news conference that the US is reviewing proposals by Turkey and India to get grain shipments moving, even as the US continues to press for a broader, negotiated settlement of the war, which is now in its fifth year. ... items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 1, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start Sunday, including G20 foreign ministers concluding their Atlanta meeting with a focus on energy security, supply chains and geopolitical tensions; clashes during nationwide protests in France; the Yemeni army’s capture of a strategic mountain range from the Houthis; and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying he agreed with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to work on establishing a new Black Sea grain corridor. G20 foreign ministers concluded two days of discussions in the US city of Atlanta focusing on energy security, global supply chain resilience and geopolitical tensions affecting international trade and economic stability, according to a statement by the US presidency. The meeting, held Oct. 30 - 31 during the 250th anniversary year of US independence, was part of Washington's effort to refocus the G20 on its core mission of addressing global economic challenges and promoting prosperity. In the chair's statement, the US presidency said the foreign ministers held "candid discussions" on Washington's priorities, including disruptions affecting strategic maritime routes such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Energy security emerged as a central theme, with the statement emphasizing the importance of affordable, abundant, and reliable energy supplies for economic growth and improved living standards. ... - Yemeni army captures strategic mountain range from Houthis in Al-Jawf The Yemeni army has completed its capture of a strategic mountain range in the northern province of Al-Jawf following battles with Houthi forces, according to a field commander. Col. Rabie al-Qurashi, an army field commander in Al-Jawf, told Anadolu that government forces secured the entire Huwayshian mountain range east of Al-Hazm, the provincial capital. He said the advance followed fighting with the Houthis and was backed by warplanes that destroyed dozens of vehicles belonging to the group. The military operation remains underway, he added. The mountains form the first line of defense for Al-Hazm, which remains under Houthi control, said al-Qurashi. - Zelenskyy says he agreed with President Erdogan to work on establishing new Black Sea grain corridor Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he had agreed with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to work on establishing a new Black Sea grain corridor. “Today, I reached an agreement with President Erdogan to work on the Black Sea grain corridor,” he said during a joint news conference in Istanbul, following talks with Erdogan. Zelenskyy said Türkiye supports efforts to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea and restore normal living conditions.

items.title: Strong growth and inflation paints mixed picture of economy days before midterm elections | | midfloridanewspapers.com
items.excerpt: - By CHRISTOPHER RUGABER AP Economics Writer #### cmarshall - Author email (cindy.marshall@highlandsnewssun.com) - Nov 1, 2026 - 5 hrs ago WASHINGTON — U.S. economic growth was notably strong from July to September, yet inflation accelerated at the same time, new data showed Thursday, painting a mixed picture about the country’s economy less than a week before midterm elections in which the uncomfortably high cost of living looms larger than perhaps any other issue. Strong consumer spending and soaring investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure were key drivers of growth in the third quarter. When unemployment is as low as it is right now, consumers often spend at a healthy clip and they are doing so, particularly wealthier Americans who are riding a wave of record stock market gains. Consumer spending climbed 3.8% at an annual rate, marking the second straight quarter of strong growth and far exceeding the 0.7% increase in the first three months of the year. Business investment, driven by spending on AI infrastructure, jumped 12.7%, the most in six years. How long can this economic growth continue? Yet economists worry that persistently high prices are eroding Americans’ ability to keep up. Thursday’s data suggest consumers are increasingly dipping into savings to cover their costs. After-tax incomes, adjusted for inflation, slipped from August to September and were up just 1% from a year earlier. At the same time, inflation-adjusted spending rose 2.5% from a year earlier. “High energy prices are chipping away at purchasing power,” Ksenia Bushmeneva, an economist at TD, a bank, wrote. “Real income failed to grow for a second consecutive month, while the saving rate continued to decline. Together with higher borrowing costs, these headwinds are likely to weigh on consumer demand in the coming quarters.” Inflation worsens Consumer prices rose 3.6% in September from a year earlier, the Commerce Department said Thursday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices climbed 0.5%, up from 0.3% in August and the highest figure since May. Rising gas prices drove much of the inflation increase as renewed violence in the Middle East kept oil prices above $100 a barrel, up from below $70 before the Iran war. But prices also rose outside of the energy sector. The cost of services such as shipping, hotel rooms, and utilities increased rapidly from August to September, a sign that inflation is spreading and growing more entrenched. The average price of a gallon of gas in the U.S. was $4.23 on Thursday, 39% more than it cost a year ago. Diesel prices have risen much faster. While most consumers don’t buy diesel, it has an outsized impact on inflation because it is used in industrial sectors and shipping. “The inflation outlook has become more concerning,” Bushmeneva said. “Price pressures are showing signs of heating up. Elevated gasoline prices are keeping headline inflation hot, but underlying pressures are also broadening.” Polls show that rising inflation has soured most voters on the economy, leading them to give President Donald Trump poor marks for his handling of rising prices. Trump campaigned in 2024 on lowering the cost of living, including bringing the cost of gas below $2 a gallon. Excluding the volatile energy and food categories, core inflation also picked up last month. It increased 3.1% from a year ago in September, up from 3% in August, the Commerce Department said. From August to September, core prices rose 0.3%, the same as the previous month. Will rising inflation raise borrowing costs? The new economic growth and inflation numbers arrive a day after the Federal Reserve, the agency tasked with combating inflation, left its key interest rate unchanged. Yet strong economic growth and persistently higher prices could mean more pain for Americans when the Fed meets in December. The Fed is now much more likely to raise its key interest rate, which could lift borrowing costs across the economy. “If the Federal Reserve is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending, historically low jobless claims, stratospheric private non-residential investment, and sizzling inflation data,” Joe Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, a tax advisory firm, wrote. Thursday’s inflation data come from the personal consumption expenditures price index, which typically echoes the better-known consumer price index published earlier this month. The Fed more closely monitors the PCE index because it puts less weight on housing prices and allows for changes in consumers’ shopping habits.

items.title: Fed’s preferred inflation gauge rose in September as third-quarter GDP beats expectations | The New York Ledger
items.excerpt: November 1, 2026 in News The Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge rose further away from the central bank’s target in September as consumers face price pressures. The Commerce Department on Thursday reported that the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index rose 0.5% on a monthly basis in September and was up 3.6% from a year ago. Both figures were in line with the expectations of economists polled by LSEG. Core PCE, which excludes volatile measurements of food and energy prices, was up 0.3% on a monthly basis and 3.1% year over year. Those figures were both in line with economists’ expectations. FEDERAL RESERVE MAKES INTEREST RATE DECISION AHEAD OF MIDTERMS Federal Reserve policymakers are focused on the PCE headline figure as they try to bring inflation back to their long-run target of 2%, though they view core data as a better indicator of inflation. Compared with August’s readings, headline PCE ticked up from 3.4% to 3.6%, while core PCE rose from 3% to 3.1%. Goods prices were up 3.9% year over year, while services prices increased 3.5% from a year ago in September. The personal savings rate as a percentage of disposable personal income was 3.8%, down from 4% in August. Over the last two years, the savings rate has declined from a peak of 6.2% in April 2025 and from 5.6% in January 2026. While inflation moved further away from the Fed’s 2% target, the Commerce Department also released the advance estimate for third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP), which grew more than expected. The Bureau of Economic Analysis estimated that third-quarter GDP was 3.4%, above the 3.2% estimate of economists polled by LSEG. The BEA will release two subsequent revisions of the third-quarter GDP data. ... ### What does it mean for the Fed and interest rates? The market continues to expect the Fed to hike interest rates by 25 basis points in December, which would bring the federal funds rate to a range of 4% to 4.25% once implemented. The CME FedWatch tool shows a 79.6% probability the Fed will hike by 25 basis points in December, down slightly from 84.2% yesterday but higher than the 73.3% probability a week ago.

items.title: Poll: Voters demand change and a check on Trump, fueling a steep Democratic midterm advantage
items.excerpt: Nov. 1, 2026, 9:00 AM EST By Ben Kamisar and Bridget Bowman Democrats have a sizable advantage in the battle for control of Congress days ahead of the midterm elections, a new national NBC News poll finds, with voters clamoring for change and voicing all-time high disapproval of President Donald Trump. Registered voters prefer a Democratic-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, with Democrats leading Republicans 52%-45% — 2 points more than in last month’s poll. That includes a 21-point lead among independents. Three percent of voters remained undecided as the poll was conducted from Oct. 28 to Oct. 30, and how they shift in the final days could tilt the outcome in dead-heat House and Senate races around the country. While the overall poll suggests that Democrats are poised to capitalize on a well of dissatisfaction with the president and his policies, there are findings that complicate the favorable picture. When it comes to which party better handles key issues, voters give Republicans and Democrats about even marks, and the Democratic Party remains deeply unpopular. Meanwhile, Republican voters in GOP-held districts and in states Trump won in 2024 are sticking with their party — notable because much of the battle for control of both the House and Senate runs through this red terrain. But there are also numerous signs of trouble for the GOP, with Trump at the center of a difficult political environment for Republicans and their slim majorities in both houses of Congress. The president’s disapproval rating has climbed to 60%, a new high mark across his two terms in the NBC News poll, and his approval rating stands at 40%. After Trump won a second term in 2024 promising to bring down prices and restore the economic conditions of his first term, roughly 3 in 4 voters head into the midterms dissatisfied with the state of the economy. Nearly two-thirds of voters are calling for a change from the direction in which Trump has been leading the country, with 50% calling for “a great deal” of change, a new high mark in NBC News polling data. And for the first time in 30 years of NBC News polling, more voters say they are dissatisfied with their financial situation (51%) than satisfied (49%). “The Trump presidency can be summarized as the promise of two years ago and the peril of two days from now,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates, who conducted the survey with Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies. Horwitt noted Trump returned to the White House after promising economic prosperity and peace. But now voters are expressing widespread concerns about the economy, with prices rising during the Iran war. Amid those concerns, 64% of voters — including a third of Trump voters — say the president has fallen short of their expectations, with 34% saying he has lived up to them. Seventy percent of voters say the country is on the wrong track, a 9-point increase over the last year. Voters continue to rank inflation and the cost of living as the most important issues facing the country, followed by government corruption, threats to democracy and immigration and border security.

items.title: Trump White House maps path to govern without Congress if Democrats win By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 1 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump’s White House has spent months preparing for a possible Democratic takeover of Congress, developing plans to keep advancing major parts of his agenda through executive power while bracing for investigations of his administration, according to a White House official and two people familiar with the plans. Senior officials, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and budget director Russell Vought, have been working with the White House Counsel’s Office since April to identify executive actions on immigration, tariffs, housing costs and federal spending that Trump could pursue without congressional approval, said the three people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. White House counsel Will Scharf and his team also are looking at "what Trump can legally do on his own, where he could push the limits of his authority and how to defend those decisions in court," the White House official said. The planning underscores a paradox of Tuesday’s midterm elections: Capturing control of Congress would give Democrats the power to investigate Trump, block legislation and constrain his spending priorities. But Trump would retain broad executive authority over trade, foreign policy and the federal bureaucracy that he has already used aggressively during his second term. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the US Senate to overturn Republicans’ narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call. For the past month, Trump has held rallies across the country trying to preserve Republican control of Congress, even as his aides privately prepare for a very different political landscape in 2027. The White House pushed back on the prospect of Republican losses and accused the media of promoting a false narrative. "This administration and commonsense Republicans will continue to secure our borders, restore law and order, putting more money back into the pockets of hard-working Americans, and deliver wins for the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said. Among the executive actions under consideration are new tariffs on imports of critical minerals and wind turbines, tighter rules on visas for international students and temporary foreign workers, and measures aimed at lowering housing and construction costs, the White House official said. Federal agencies have submitted proposals and legal reviews of actions the administration could take unilaterally, one of the people with knowledge of the plans said. Vought, whose US Office of Management and Budget oversees federal spending, is examining which priorities can move forward using money already appropriated by Congress, two of the people said. He also wants to change federal grant rules to give political appointees more say in which government programs receive taxpayer money, they said, potentially giving the White House more influence over federal spending without seeking congressional approval. Trump has been briefed on the preparations and has taken part in discussions about them, the White House official said. When asked how comfortable Trump would be governing through executive authority under a Democratic Congress, one of the people said, "very comfortable." ... Trump has already tested the reach of presidential power since returning to office in January 2025, using executive authority to impose sweeping tariffs, intensify immigration enforcement, shrink the federal workforce, and pursue foreign-policy goals including the war against Iran without Congress’ approval or new laws. A major exception was Trump’s massive package of tax and spending cuts that was passed by the Republican-controlled Congress and signed into law by the president in July 2025. "President Trump in the last two years has basically ignored Congress and tried to do as much as possible through executive orders and executive power," said Nathan Gonzales, editor at Inside Elections, which provides nonpartisan political analysis. "I think he will only continue if there are Democratic majorities." Trump has repeatedly invoked national emergencies to expand his ability to act without new legislation. Congress can vote to end those emergencies, but Trump could veto such a move, requiring two-thirds majorities in both chambers to override him. A Democratic Congress could still create significant obstacles. Control of the Senate would allow Democrats to block Trump’s judicial and executive-branch nominees, including any Supreme Court pick. "I would anticipate they will be very reluctant to approve any of the president’s appointments," said Andrew Busch, a public policy professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, and author of a history of midterm elections. Democrats could also refuse to pass Trump-backed legislation. But Trump could veto Democratic legislation he doesn’t like, and Democrats are unlikely to have enough votes in the House to override him. Courts could block executive actions that exceed Trump’s legal authority. The White House plans to seek legal opinions from the Justice Department to determine what Trump can do without Congress and how to defend those actions if they are challenged in court, one of the people said. ... One challenge, however, cannot be sidestepped through executive action: congressional investigations. Reuters previously reported that senior House Democrats and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document requests to examine whether Trump has used his presidential power to benefit himself, allies or donors. items.excerpt: ### Patrick Stewart’s final role, Cate Blanchett in Tokyo, Jailer 2 closes in on ₹800 crore & Nollywood’s ₦400 million October. ... Patrick Stewart’s farewell performance: Marvel Studios has confirmed that Avengers: Doomsday, which opens on 18 December, will be Sir Patrick Stewart’s final onscreen performance, which ends a 26-year run as Professor Xavier. It means he won’t appear in the already-filmed content for Avengers: Secret Wars. He appears opposite Sir Ian McKellen’s Magneto, and the pair have already appeared together in the trailers. McKellen’s tribute, in which he said Stewart wore his heart on his sleeve and was a man to rely on, to admire and, in his case, to love, ended by noting that Stewart’s farewell performance in Avengers: Doomsday is yet to be seen. McKellen recalled that when Stewart first told him about a Star Trek offer, he urged him to think of his stage career, which is advice that Stewart, happily for the rest of us, ignored. McKellen also officiated at Stewart’s 2013 wedding. Hugh Jackman, who played Wolverine opposite Stewart’s Professor X, called him one of the greats of stage and screen, and Rebecca Romijn thanked him as a fellow mutant and a fellow member of Starfleet. The Far East: Cate Blanchett in Tokyo: At the Tokyo International Film Festival on Friday, the first five short films made through Cate Blanchett’s Displacement Film Fund were screened, with Blanchett joined for a Q&A by the fund’s directors Shahrbanoo Sadat and Mohammad Rasoulof, and with help from Perfect Days actor Kōji Yakusho. Sadat’s feature No Good Men was also at the London Film Festival this month. The festival runs until 4 November. Tamil cinema: Jailer 2 closes in on ₹800 crore: Rajinikanth’s Jailer 2 stands at ₹776.95 crore (about $81 million) worldwide and ₹435.4 crore net (about $45 million) in India after 16 days, according to Sacnilk, and it’s closing in on the ₹800 crore milestone. Its ₹509.45 crore gross in India is within ₹10 crore of the all-time Tamil record in India, held by 2.0. I’ll bring you the full third-weekend numbers tomorrow. Nollywood’s ₦400 million October: In Nigeria, faith-based hit Agbara Nla: The Return topped the chart for a fourth weekend with ₦32.8 million (about $25,000) from 5,477 admissions over 23–25 October, taking it to ₦408.3 million (about $307,000), which makes it the first October release ever to pass ₦400 million. By Thursday its total had reached ₦422.7 million (about $318,000). Among the new releases, the campus drama Tele x Zikora, directed by Adenike Adebayo-Esho, had the biggest opening with ₦26.9 million (about $20,000), while Clayface opened fourth with ₦16.8 million (about $13,000). Fusion Intelligence expects 2026 to pass the whole of 2025’s Nigerian box office total early this month, helped by higher ticket prices. Birthdays: Toni Collette, star of The Sixth Sense and Hereditary, turns 54 today, and Aishwarya Rai Bachchan of Devdas turns 53. Also celebrating is Rob Riggle (56), who stars in Christmas at the Kringles, which opened in US cinemas on Friday.

items.excerpt: - Nov 1, 2026 - Nov 1, 2026 Updated 7 hrs ago Heidi Klum reveals Halloween costume as her iconic party marks 25 years Heidi Klum underwent a bloody transformation to become a giant, gruesome severed hand for Halloween. Klum unveiled her costume Saturday as her iconic costume party marked 25 years in New York. Klum was unrecognizable with only her eyes and mouth showing, blood dripping from her mouth as she stuck her tongue out. The top of the hand ended in a gory assortment of dangling ligaments and tendons. She had an ensemble of helpers in blood-stained hazmat suits. The supermodel-turned-TV personality went viral in 2022 when she arrived at the party on the end of a fishing line, encased in a slithering worm costume. Houdini’s centennial spotlight: A newly published essay and a fresh fight over when and how he died NEW YORK (AP) — Harry Houdini, a century after his death, continues to captivate. A rare essay by the escape artist has been published, shedding light on his early influences. A recent book revisits questions about the cause and date of his death. Houdini, born Erik Weisz, became an international celebrity known for his escape acts. His mysterious death on Halloween 1926 remains debated, with new theories challenging the official cause. Centennial events this weekend include a "Grand Houdini Centenarium" in Budapest, an auction in Hollywood, and seances in Chicago and Maryland. Despite the intrigue, experts say his legacy endures through his remarkable life. Scott Clifton and Tamara Tunie earn lead acting Daytime Emmys. 'General Hospital' wins again LOS ANGELES (AP) — Scott Clifton of “The Bold and the Beautiful” and Tamara Tunie of “Beyond the Gates” have won lead acting honors at the Daytime Emmy Awards. It's Clifton's second career trophy in the lead category. Tunie made her return to the soap opera genre after 17 years away. “General Hospital” won its record 19th trophy overall as outstanding drama and sixth in a row. Roger Howarth and Beth Maitland of “The Young and the Restless” swept the supporting acting categories. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, lost in the lifestyle program category for her former Netflix show “With Love, Meghan.” Margaret Qualley, Jack Antonoff file for divorce after 3 years of marriage NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Margaret Qualley and Grammy winner Jack Antonoff have filed for divorce after three years of marriage. Court records show the case was filed Friday in Kings County Supreme Court in New York as an uncontested matrimonial action. Qualley is listed as the plaintiff, and Antonoff as the defendant. The couple separated in July. Qualley, 32, is known for films like “The Substance” and “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” Antonoff, 42, is a 14-time Grammy-winning songwriter and producer. The couple began dating in 2021 and married in August 2023. An introspective Kirk Franklin is no longer apologizing with 'I Am What I Am' album NEW YORK (AP) — Kirk Franklin is back with his new album, "I Am What I Am," out Friday. His 14th studio project and first double album, 14 tracks are divided between contemporary music and traditional, live-recorded gospel songs. Features include gospel royalty Karen Clark Sheard and star mainstream artists like Jelly Roll, Davido and GloRilla. “This Time," featuring GloRilla, hit No. 1 on Billboard’s hot gospel songs, extending Franklin's record to ten No. 1s on the chart. Known for his crossover hits, the 20-time Grammy winner has frequently faced criticism for working with secular artists, but remains unapologetic in the name of spreading his Christian faith. 'Time is the fire in which we burn': 2 major cast losses rock the passionate 'Star Trek' universe WASHINGTON (AP) — First Walter Koenig, who played Ensign Pavel Chekov in the original series during the 1960s, died at age 90. Then, three days later, the cosmos lost Patrick Stewart. The Shakespearean actor in 1987 became Capt. Jean-Luc Picard, the unlikely and poetic face of that show’s sequel, “Star Trek: The Next Generation.” For a fan base that has long signed on as acolytes of a brighter, more equitable future, recent days have made the present sting. William Shatner played Capt. James T. Kirk in the original series in the 1960s. He called it a “heartbreaking week.” Patrick Stewart found 'Star Trek' fame but always returned to Shakespeare and the stage LONDON (AP) — Before he captained the Starship Enterprise, Patrick Stewart commanded the Shakespearean stage. And it was the stage to which he returned time and again, even after “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and “X-Men” made him a Hollywood star. Stewart was a celebrated Shakespearean actor, spending over 15 years with the Royal Shakespeare Company. The company's former artistic director called him “a true Shakespearean.” Stewart's passion for theater began in ... Prosecutors drop felony charge against rapper Rick Ross in domestic violence case MIAMI BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Prosecutors have dropped a felony charge against rapper Rick Ross a month after he was arrested in Miami Beach when a woman he was living with told police he hit her. The Miami-Dade State Attorney’s Office filed paperwork Thursday to drop a felony charge of battery by strangulation because of “insufficient evidence.” Ross, whose legal name is William Roberts II, still faces a misdemeanor charge of battery domestic violence. Ross has pleaded not guilty to all charges. Officials say Ross surrendered at the Miami Beach police station on Oct. 1, two days after the woman filed a report with police. Patrick Stewart, legendary actor of ‘Star Trek’ and 'X-Men' fame, dies at 86 Patrick Stewart, the classically trained stage actor who scaled the Shakespearean canon and added gravitas to a “Star Trek” franchise and the “X-Men” films, has died. He was 86. A spokesperson said Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia. Stewart was best known as Professor Charles Xavier from the “X-Men” and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from “Star Trek: The Next Generation,” but he spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise.
